en: Salutation to Brahman, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest, who is devoid of qualities yet is the essence of all qualities, and whose body is the support of the entire universe.
When only a small portion remained of what was to be done, a great asura named Maya,
desiring to know the supreme secret and the highest knowledge, [approached].
Worshiping Vivasvat, he performed most difficult austerities, [practicing] the entirety of that foremost limb of the Vedas which is the cause for the movement of the luminaries.
Satisfied by that asceticism and pleased with him who sought a boon,
Savitṛ himself bestowed upon Maya the course of the planets.
1.05a: "My disposition is known to you by me, for I have been gratified by your asceticism;
1.05b: I shall grant you the knowledge based on time and the great movements of the planets."
"No one has the power to describe my splendor, nor do I have the leisure;
this man, who is a portion of myself, will explain it to you in its entirety."
Having spoken thus and assigned his own portion, the God vanished;
that Puruṣa then spoke this to Maya, who stood with palms joined in reverence.
Listen with a focused mind to that supreme knowledge which was formerly spoken by Vivasvat himself, in age after age, to the great seers.
1.09a: This very same scripture is that which Bhāskara previously proclaimed;
1.09b: here there is only a difference of time due to the revolution of the ages (yugas).
1.10a: Time is the destroyer of worlds; time is other than that which consists of calculation.
1.10b: It is twofold due to its gross and subtle nature; it is called both "embodied" (mūrta) and "unembodied" (amūrta).
1.11a: That which begins with *prāṇa* is called "embodied" (*mūrta*), while that which begins with *truṭi* is designated as "unembodied" (*amūrta*).
1.11b: Six *prāṇas* constitute a *vināḍī*, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā*.
1.12a: A sidereal day and night is proclaimed to consist of sixty nāḍīs;
1.12b: thirty of those constitute a month, as does a solar month measured by the risings of the sun.

1.13a: Likewise, a lunar month is said to consist of [thirty] lunar days (tithis), and a solar month is said to consist of a single transit (saṃkrānti). 1.13b: Twelve months constitute a year, which is called a divine day.
1.14a: For the gods and the asuras, a day and night are reversed from one another.
1.14b: Sixty times that, multiplied by six, is a divine year and likewise an asura year.
1.15a: Twelve thousand of those [years] are declared to be a cycle of four ages (caturyuga).
1.15b: By the number of solar years, it is multiplied by twenty-three oceans (230,000) and ten thousand (10,000).
1.16a: Together with their respective twilights and twilight-periods, that constitutes a cycle of four yugas;
1.16b: this is the established order of the Kṛta and the other ages, according to the arrangement of the quarters of Dharma.

The tenth part of the Yuga, multiplied respectively by four, three, two, and one, constitutes the duration of the Kṛta Yuga and the others; each of these has its own two junctions (sandhyās), which are each one-sixth of that period.
1.18a: Seventy-one yugas are here called a manvantara.
1.18b: At its end, the number of years of the Kṛta age is said to be the transitional period (sandhi), which is a deluge of water.

1.19a: These fourteen Manus, together with the transitional periods (*sandhi*), are to be known as belonging to a *kalpa*. 1.19b: At the beginning of the *kalpa*, the transitional period is recorded as being fifteen times the measure of the *Kṛta* age.
1.20a: Thus, by a thousand yugas, the period that effects the destruction of beings is called a *kalpa*, which is a day of Brahmā; his night is of equal duration.
1.21a: One hundred years is the maximum lifespan according to that reckoning of days and nights.
1.21b: Half of his lifespan has passed; this is the first remaining kalpa.
1.22a: Six Manus, along with their transitional periods, have passed from this kalpa;
1.22b: and of the Vaivasvata Manu, three cycles of four ages (yugas) have elapsed.
1.23a: From this twenty-eighth yuga, this Kṛtayuga has passed;
1.23b: having calculated the time from here, one should sum the numbers together into one total.
1.24: While he was creating the moving and unmoving world—including the planets, stars, gods, and demons—one hundred times four hundred and thirty-two divine years have passed for the Creator.
Moving westward with extreme speed, the planets are constantly overtaken by the lunar mansions;
yet, remaining on their own orbits, they lag behind at exactly the same rate.
1.26a: Therefore, their motion is eastward; their daily motion [is determined] by the [sidereal] revolutions.
1.26b: It differs according to their circumferences, and by virtue of that, they traverse the asterisms.
1.27a: Then, the fast-moving [planet] completes them in a short time, while the slow-moving one does so in a long time.
1.27b: By the revolution of these [revolutions], the bhagaṇa (the full cycle of revolutions) is traditionally reckoned as ending with the asterism of Puṣya.
1.28a: A sixtieth part of a *vikalā* is called a *kalā*; sixty of those constitute a *rāśi*. 1.28b: Thirty of those make a *bhagaṇa*, and there are twelve of these [in a cycle].
In a yuga, the number of revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus are 4,320,000;
those of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, moving eastward, are as follows: [4,320,000; 2,296,824; and 3,64,220].
1.30a: For Mercury (Indu), the values are the juices (6), fires (3), tris (3), arrows (5), saptas (7), mountains (7), and paths (4).
(57753336) 1.30b: For Mars (Kuja), however, they are the dasras (2), tris (3), aṣṭas (8), rasas (6), aṅkas (9), eyes (2), and locanas (2).

1.31b: For Bṛhaspati, [the revolutions] are thirty-six thousand, two hundred and twenty;

1.33a: For the Moon's apogee, [the values] in the six periods (yuga) are fire, zero, horse, bull, wealth, and serpent-oceans:
(4, 8, 20, 3). 1.33b: To the left of the node (pāta), they are wealth, fire, Yama, horse, crest-jewel, and snake: (2, 3, 2, 2, 1, 13). 1.34a:
For the [mean] longitudes of the planets, they are eight, eye, horse, wealth, mountain, three, two, two, eight, arrow, and moon: (15, 8, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 1).
1.34b: In a Yuga, the respective right ascensions are [obtained] by subtracting their own respective revolutions from their own [sidereal] revolutions.
The lunar months are the difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon;
those [lunar months], when diminished by the solar months, are the remaining intercalary months.
1.36a: Having subtracted the lunar day-deficiencies from the lunar days, [one obtains] the solar days;
1.36b: from one sunrise to the next sunrise is a terrestrial civil day (bhūsāvanavāsara).
In a *yuga*, the lunar months are 1,577,917,828, equal to the digits of the verse "vasu-dvi-aṣṭa-adri-rūpa-aṅka-sapta-adri-tithayaḥ" (1-2-8-7-7-15).

The intercalary months (*adhimāsaka*) are 1,593,336, equal to the digits of the verse "ṣaṭ-vahni-tri-hutāśa-aṅka-tithayaḥ" (6-3-3-9-15). The solar days are 1,603,000,080, equal to the digits of the verse "khāṣṭa-khakhavyoma-khāgni-khartu-niśākarāḥ" (0-8-0-0-0-3-6-1).

1.38b: The lunar day-decrements (tithikṣaya) are 25,082,252. 1.39a: The solar months are 51,840,000, being [the sum of] zero, four, ocean, eight, earth, five, and sun. 1.39b: When subtracted by the revolutions of the sun, these become the days of the mean moon (bhodayāḥ).
1.40a: Adhimāsa days, lunar nights, nakṣatras, lunar days, and civil days;
1.40b: these, when multiplied by a thousand, become the revolutions and so forth in a Kalpa.
1.41a: In the *kalpa* of the solar mandala that has passed, [the revolutions] of Mars are seven, eight, and three fires (387);
1.41b: those of Mercury are four, sky, and two moons (204), and those of Jupiter are eight, seasons, and fires (368).
1.42a: Those of Venus are sky, arrows, and cavities (900), and those of Saturn are objects, qualities, and arrows (535).
1.42b: For Saturn and Rāhu, [the revolutions] are 1,420; for the nodes, they are to the left.

For Jupiter, 173; and likewise for Venus, 533.
The number of revolutions of Saturn’s apogee in a kalpa is six hundred and sixty-two (662).
1.44b: The revolutions of the Moon’s apogee and node have already been stated here previously.

1.45a: Having compressed together the duration of the six Manus along with their respective junctions (sandhis), 1.45b: as well as the junction at the beginning of the Kalpa and likewise that of Vaivasvata Manu.
1.46a: Three times the cube of the number of Yugas have passed, as has this present Kṛtayuga;
1.46b: having subtracted from that the time since creation previously stated according to divine reckoning.
1.47a: These [yugas] are to be known as having passed at the end of the Kṛta age by the number of solar years.

1.48a: From this point onward, these [current yugas] are joined with the number of years of elapsed time. 1.48b: Converted into months, they are further added to the months that have passed since the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
1.49a: Those [mean] days, multiplied by the intercalary months and divided by the solar months, yield the intercalary months;
1.49b: when added to the [mean] days converted into days and increased by those obtained intercalary months.
1.50a: The [mean] lunar days, doubled and multiplied by the *tithi*-defects, are divided by the number of lunar days;
1.50b: subtracting the resulting omitted nights, these are the midnight [mean] times at Laṅkā.
1.51a: The solar day-count is derived from the Sun; from that, the days, months, and years are obtained.
1.51b: Divided by seven, the remainder is the lord of the day, beginning with the Sun.
1.52a: Divided by the number of months and years in days, multiplied by two or three, and increased by one;
1.52b: the remainders after being divided by seven are to be known as the [corrected] months and years.
Just as the accumulated number of revolutions multiplied by the days is divided by the elapsed days, so the planet, beginning with its revolutions, is obtained through its mean motion.
1.54a: Thus, those [planets] whose own swifter and slower apogees were previously stated as moving forward; 1.54b:
the nodes (pātas), having a retrograde motion, are likewise subtracted from the circle (the zodiac).
The completed revolutions of Jupiter, multiplied by twelve and added to the current signs,
when divided by sixty, yield the *vijayā* days and so forth.

1.56a: This has been explained in detail; now, the practical method for calculating the mean positions of the planets from the desired epoch shall be stated in brief. 1.56b: The calculation of the mean [positions] of the planets must be performed according to the desired starting point of the Yuga.

1.57a: At the end of this Kṛtayuga, all the planets, with the exception of the nodes and apogees, have reached equality at the beginning of Aries (the first point of the zodiac). 1.57b: [This occurs] together with the moon.
In Capricorn and the following signs, the Moon is at its highest point; however, its *pāta* (node) is in Libra and the following signs.
Others have reached a state of being without degrees (*niraṃśatva*), and thus they are not mentioned as having slow motion.
The diagonal of the earth is eight hundred yojanas, doubled [to sixteen hundred]. The square root of ten times its square shall be the circumference of the earth.
1.60a: One's own mean circumference of the earth, multiplied by the sine of the colatitude and divided by the radius, becomes the true circumference.
1.60b: The daily motion of a planet, multiplied by the longitudinal difference [in yojanas] and divided by that [true circumference], yields the correction for longitude.
1.61a: One should subtract that result, beginning with the *kalās*, from the [longitude of the] planets in the eastern direction;
1.61b: one should add it when situated in the western direction of the meridians (*rekhā*); thus they become those produced for one's own location (*svadeśaja*).
1.62a: Those situated on the central meridian between the abode of the Rākṣasas and the realm of the gods, such as Rohītaka and Avantī, are like a nearby lake. 1.62b: [They are] like a nearby lake.
1.63a: When, due to the emergence [of the moon] having passed beyond that point calculated from the [previous] moon, 1.63b:
it occurs in the east, then its true position would be at the center.
1.64a: And if [the conjunction] has not yet been reached, it will occur later; likewise, due to the closing [of the day], 1.64b:
one should multiply the true circumference of the earth by the nadīs between those two [times].

1.65a: Having divided by sixty, the result in *yojanas*—both to the east and to the west—is to be known as one's own location on the circumference; for one should apply the difference of place (*deśāntara*) by means of those [yojanas].
1.66a: In the eastern region, the commencement of the weekday occurs at midnight when [the time] is exceeded by the local longitudinal difference (*deśāntara*) in nāḍīs.
1.66b: In the western region, one should indicate it as occurring when [the time] is deficient by those same *deśāntara* nāḍīs.
1.67a: The motion multiplied by the elapsed nāḍīs and divided by sixty yields the result in minutes (kalās) and so forth.
1.67b: Having subtracted this from the [longitude] already traversed, or added it to that yet to be traversed, the [longitude] for the specific time (tātkālika) is obtained.
1.68a: The Moon is displaced by its own apsis to a maximum of eighty-sixth parts of the zodiacal circle toward the south or north.
1.68b: [This displacement occurs] from the limit of its own [mean] declination.
The ninth part of that [longitude] is doubled for Jupiter, tripled for Mars, and quadrupled for Mercury, Venus, and Saturn; these are then subtracted by the nodes (pātas).
1.70a: Thus, three, nine, nine, zero, twelve, twelve, six, and twelve, multiplied by ten;
1.70b: these are stated in order as the seconds of the middle equation of anomaly for the Moon and the other planets.
[The Chapter on Planetary Visibility] 2.01a:

The forms of time, which are invisible and reside within the celestial spheres (bhagaṇa), are known as the apogees of mean motion (śīghrocca) and the apogees of slow motion (mandocca), as well as the nodes (pāta); they are the causes of the motion of the planets. 2.01b: [End of verse]
2.02a: Bound by those [rays] with their left and right hands, 2.02b:
they are drawn forward and backward according to their proximity, facing their own respective directions.
2.03a: The wind named Pravaha impels them toward their respective exaltations; 2.03b: drawn back and forth by the east and west, they move in various ways.

2.04a: When situated in the first half of the zodiacal circle from the apogee, [the anomaly] pulls the planet toward the east; 2.04b: When situated in the latter half, known as the apsis (*ucca*), it likewise pulls the planet toward the west.
2.05a: Since the planets move eastward at speeds subtracted from their [mean] revolutions by their own [longitude] exaltations (*svoccāpakṛṣṭā bhagaṇaiḥ*), 2.05b:
that is said to be a "plus" (*dhana*) in those [planets], and a "minus" (*ṛṇa*) in those moving westward. 2.06a: Likewise, the node Rāhu, by its own velocity, [moves] to the south and north.
In the south and north,
Rāhu, by his great speed,
causes the displacement of the moon and other bodies through their deviation from their course.
2.07a: Moving in the latter half [of its orbit], the planet situated in the eastern half of the circle draws the [mean] planet toward the north at dawn.
2.07b: Situated in the eastern half of the circle, it pulls the planet toward the south.
2.08a: When the node (*pāta*) is situated in the same manner relative to the swifter of Mercury and Venus, 2.08b:
those two [planets] are displaced as previously described due to the attraction of that swifter [node].
2.09a: Because of its great size, the sun is drawn back only a very short distance from the [ecliptic] circle;
2.09b: because of its small size, the moon is therefore drawn back a much greater distance from the circle.
2.10a: Mars and the others, due to their small physical forms, [are affected] by those known as the fast and slow apogees (or nodes).
2.10b: They are drawn away to a very great distance by the deities with extreme velocity.
2.11a: Therefore, by virtue of their movement, there arises for them a very great debt of merit and demerit.
2.11b: Thus, being dragged along by those very [forces] and struck by the wind, they travel through the sky.
2.12a: Retrograde, direct-retrograde, deficient, slow, slower, and uniform;
(C: retrograde and sub-direct); 2.12b: as well as faster and fast—such is the eightfold motion of the planets.

2.13a: Therein, [the gait] is known to be fivefold: very swift, swift, slow, slower, and even; 2.13b: that which is straight is [the fifth], while the crooked one moves in an excessively curved manner.
(And others are considered to be [orbits] such as the eccentric [vakrā], etc. 2.14a:

I shall now explain with care that process of rectification by which the planets constantly attain equality of aspect through the power of their respective motions. 2.14b: I shall explain that process of rectification with due respect.

2.15a: One-eighth of the minutes of arc of the zodiacal sign is called the first half-chord (jyārdha). 2.15b: That [first half-chord], increased by the quotient obtained from dividing it by that same [number] and subtracted from itself, is the second [half-chord].

2.16a: Having thus divided the *piṇḍas* by the first [number] in sequence, [the results] are joined with the quotient subtracted from [the original]; 2.16b: these shall be the segments, the twenty-four half-chord sums (*jyārdhapiṇḍas*) in order.
2.17a: The [results] for the *khaṇḍakas* are 224, 449, and 691, derived from the true *aśvinī* [value] by multiplying with the [coefficients] four, one, and four; and 1, 7, 6, and 6.
2.17b: [The results] are 890, 1105, and 1315, derived from zero, nine, eight, five, zero, eleven, five, one, and one.

2.21b: Yama, mountain, fire, and flame; void, zero, ocean, and fire (3372, 3401).

2.26b: Vasus, oceans, objects, twins, horses, seasons, mountains, and Aśvins (2548, 2767).
2.27a: Nine, eight, nine, and eyes; fire, one, Yama, and fires (2989, 3293).
2.27b: The half-sums of the sines of successive increments are [multiplied] by the qualities of elephants, fire, and oceans (864).
2.28a: But the maximum sine of declination is the moon multiplied by the apertures and the sense organs (1397).
2.28b: A sine multiplied by that [maximum] and divided by the radius-sine (trijīvā), its arc is called the declination (krānti). (This is desired.)
2.29a: Having subtracted the apogee from the planet, and likewise having subtracted it from the perigee;
2.29b: the remainder is the *kendra* (anomalistic distance) and its quadrant-position (*pada*); from that, one obtains the sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) and the cosine (*koṭi*).
In an odd quadrant, the sine of the arc traversed shall be the arm-sine (*bhuja-jyā*), and the sine of the arc yet to be traversed shall be the cosine (*koṭi*).
In an even quadrant, however, the sine of the arc yet to be traversed shall be the arm-sine, and the sine of the arc traversed shall be the cosine.
2.31a: Divided by the products of the principles and the yamas, the quotient obtained is the arc-sine (*jyāpiṇḍikā*) of the traversed [degrees].
2.31b: One should multiply the difference between the traversed and the remaining [degrees] and divide by the eyes of the principles (*tattvalocana*). (225)
2.32a: That [result], having obtained its fruit, should be added to the aggregate of sines known as the "traversed" (*gata*).
2.32b: This rule for sequential sines (*kramajyā*) is also prescribed for inverse sines (*utkramajyā*).

2.33a: Having subtracted the string from the remainder, that [remainder] is multiplied by the number of principles (tattva) minus two, and divided by their difference; (C: having subtracted the other, and multiplied by the number of principles plus two). 2.33b: Having added [the result] to the product of the number of principles and eighteen, it is called the bow (dhanus).
2.34a: The degrees of the Sun's minimum circumference are fourteen; those of the Moon are thirty-two. 3.34b:
At the end of even signs, these values are increased by twenty; at the end of odd signs, they are decreased by twenty.
2.35a: At the end of the even [verses], the numbers are two, three, zero, fire, gods, sun, nine, and oceans: (2, 30, 33, 12, 49). 2.35b:
In the odd [verses], they are two, eight, eight, wealth, Yama, teeth, Rudras, elephants, and years: (2, 8, 8, 18, 11, 32, 14, 11, 4).
2.36a: From this point, the [mean] longitudes of Mars and the other planets at the end of the even sign are the swift [parameters]: 133, 70, 262, and 39.
[The corrections for] the swift motion are 133, 70, 262, and 39. (Alternatively, they are 0, 70, 262, and 39.)
2.37a: At the end of the *ojā* [padas], there are two, three, and one *yama*s; two, all [four], and the Yama-mountains (*yamaparvata*s).
(C: two, three, and *yama*s) 2.37b:
Sky, twice ten, and sky-quadruples are proclaimed in the calculation of mean motion (*śīghrakarman*).
2.38a: The sine of the arc (bhujajyā) is the product of the odd-numbered and even-numbered intervals multiplied together, divided by the radius (trijyā).
2.38b: In an even circle, it shall be positive or negative; in an odd one, it is clearly [determined] when [the value] is less than or greater than [the previous].
The sines of the [mean] anomaly's arc and its complement are multiplied by that [mean anomaly] and divided by the degrees in a circle (360).
The arc of the resulting sine of the anomaly is the manda-phala, expressed in minutes of arc and so forth.
2.40a: The result of the cotangent (koṭiphala) in the odd quadrants beginning with Capricorn is known as velocity (śaighrya) and is considered positive.
2.40b: However, in the even quadrants beginning with Cancer, the result derived from the cotangent is to be subtracted from the radius (trijīvā).
2.41a: The square root of the sum of the squares of that [result] and the sine-result (bāhuphala) is the hypotenuse (karṇa), which is called "moving" (cala).
The result of the arc-sine (bhujaphala), multiplied by the radius (trijyā) and divided by the eccentric radius (calakarṇa).
2.42a: The arc of the obtained [equation of center], converted into minutes of arc and so forth, is known as this "quickness" (*śaighrya*).
2.42b: This applies to Mars and the other planets in the first and the fourth operations.
2.43a: One slow motion (*mānda*) for the Sun and Moon; now that of Mars and the others is being stated.
2.43b: Swift, slow, again slow, and swift—these four [motions] follow in sequence.
2.44a: In the middle [of the calculation], half of the swift correction (*śīghraphala*) is the slow correction (*mānda*), and likewise half of that result is the [next] slow correction.
2.44b: At the mean conjunction, the slow correction (*manda-phala*) is complete, as is the swift correction (*śaighrya*).

Furthermore, when all [planets] are in the Aries and other signs of the eastern quadrant, and when they are in their state of swiftness (*śaighrya*) and in the slow motion (*mānda*) operation: (C: when they are in the slow motion and in the state of swiftness).
2.45b: The wealth of the planets, expressed in minutes of arc and so forth, is indeed a debt in the case of Libra and the subsequent signs.
The motion of a planet, multiplied by twelve hundred and sixty and divided by the number of zodiacal signs,
should be converted into minutes of arc for the planet, just as in the case of the sun.
2.47a: The mean motion of the Moon, corrected by its own [mean] slow motion, 2.47b:
having performed the calculation of the difference of the sine of the arm and so forth, shall result in [the true] motion as either a debt or a credit.

2.48a: The result for the planetary motion should be calculated as in the case of a planet during the slow-motion operation (*mandakarma*). 2.48b: The motion (*bhukti*) multiplied by the difference of the sines of the arms (*dorjyāntara*), and divided again by twenty-seven (*tattvanetra*), 2.49a: [is] multiplied by its own slow-circumference (*svamandaparidhi*) and divided by the degrees in a circle (*bhagaṇāṃśa*), [yielding] minutes of arc (*kalā*).
2.49b: However, in the case of Cancer and the following signs, there is wealth; in the case of Capricorn and the following, it is traditionally held that there is debt.
2.50a: Having subtracted the mean velocity made manifest (the manda-sphuta-bhukti) from the velocity of the swift apogee (śīghrocca-bhukti);
2.50b: one should then multiply that remainder by the difference between the trijyā and the final karṇa.
2.51a: When the [true] anomaly is greater than the radius, the correction derived from the moving ear (calakarṇa) is positive for the equation of motion; when it is less, it is negative.
2.51b: When [the true anomaly] is greater, subtracting the remainder results in retrograde motion.
2.52a: When a planet situated at a distance from its own swiftest apogee is drawn by loosened rays [of light], 2.52b: its body being pulled to the left or right, it then undergoes retrograde motion.
2.53a: By [the numbers] 164, 144, 130, and 83, which correspond to the seasons (6), the moon (1), the Vedas (4), Indra (14), zero, three, one, and the qualities (3) and eight;
2.53b: and by 115, which corresponds to the arrows (5) and Rudras (11), [the planets] beginning with Mars occupy the degrees of the quadrants (kendras) in the fourth [houses].
2.54a: They become retrograde when subtracted from their respective zodiacal circles (cakras).
2.54b: By means of their own kendras equal to the remaining degrees, they abandon their retrograde motion.
2.55a: Due to the greatness of its swift circumference, Venus and Mars are in the seventh house;
2.55b: Jupiter and the Moon are in the eighth, while Saturn is in the ninth.
2.56a: For Mars, the Sun, Jupiter, and the nodes, the result arising from the swift [equation] is like that of the planets.
2.56b: For Mercury and Venus, the third result, arising from the slow [equation], is retrograde.
2.57a: From the planet [calculated] from its own pāta, the sine (jīvā) is derived; for Venus and Mercury, it is from the [longitude] corrected by the equation of center (śīghra).

2.57b: Multiplied by the eccentricity (vikṣepa) and divided by the final radius (antyakarṇa), this is the latitude (vikṣepa); for the Moon, it is divided by the radius of the trigonometric circle (trijyā).
2.58a: When the direction of the declination and the obliquity are the same, the obliquity is added to the declination;
2.58b: when their directions differ, it is subtracted; thus the true [obliquity] is obtained, just as that of the Sun.
The daily motion [of a planet] multiplied by the breaths in the rising period (udayaprāṇa) and divided by one thousand eight hundred is the number of breaths in a zodiacal circle (cakrāsava).
When added to the quotient, these are known as the breaths in its own day-and-night (svāhorātrāsava).

2.60a: Having computed both the forward and reverse sines of the traversed [arc], one should subtract the reverse sine from the radius (trijyā) therein; that is the half-diameter of the day-circle in the southern or northern hemisphere.
2.60b: That is the half-diameter of the day-circle in the southern or northern hemisphere.
2.61a: The equinoctial shadow multiplied by the declination sine and divided by twelve is the latitude sine.
2.61b: Multiplied by the radius and divided by the semi-diurnal hypotenuse, it yields the carajāsava (ascensional difference in time-units).
2.62a: That bow [is used] during the rising [of the sun]; when wealth and power are situated separately, there is loss of wealth.
2.62b: A fourth part of its own day-and-night is known as the half of the day and the half of the night.
2.63a: When the southern declination is reversed and doubled, the day and night [are determined]; 2.63b:
by means of that declination increased or decreased by the [maximum] deviation, the [lengths of] the shadows of the sun are likewise [found].
2.64a: The true motion [of a planet] is eight hundred and sixty liptās; likewise, the [longitude of the] lunar day is seven hundred and thirty.
2.64b: The signs [traversed] are obtained by dividing the planet's liptās by its true motion; from the daily motion, the days and so forth are calculated.
2.65a: From the minutes of the conjunction of the Sun and the Moon, the yogas are obtained by dividing by the [longitude of the] asterism's duration (bhabhoga).
2.65b: These are the elapsed and remaining [yogas], multiplied by sixty and divided by the sum of their motions, yielding the nāḍīs.
2.66a: From the degrees of the moon subtracted by those of the sun, the tithis are obtained by dividing by the [daily] motion.
2.66b: Those elapsed and those yet to come, multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in motion, yield the nāḍīs.
2.67a: Dhruva, Śakuni, and Nāga as the third, along with Catuṣpada;
2.67b: and Kiṃstughna, starting from the latter half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
2.68a: Following those, there are seven others beginning with Bava, known as the *cara* (movable) *karaṇas*.
2.68b: Each one of these *karaṇas* occurs eight times in a month.
2.69a: One should calculate the enjoyment of half a lunar day for all the *karaṇas*.
2.69b: This is declared to be the true motion of the celestial wanderers, beginning with the Sun.

3.01a: On a surface of stone purified by water, or even on a level floor smeared with diamond-paste (vajralepa), 3.01b: there one should draw a circular mandala of equal size using desired finger-breadths measured by a śaṅku-stake.
3.02a: One should place a gnomon twelve finger-breadths long in the center of that.
3.02b: Wherever the tip of its shadow touches the circle during the first and second halves of the day, [one should mark those points].
3.03a: Having placed two dots there within a circle designated as "east" and "west," 3.03b:
a line representing a fish-tail (timinī) must be drawn between them, running from south to north.
3.04a: Between the southern and northern directions, the east-west direction is established by means of the *timi* fish;
3.04b: likewise, the intermediate directions are determined by means of the *matsya* fish situated between those directions.
3.05a: One should draw a square on the outside with lines extending from the center;
3.05b: when the desired radiance is provided there by means of the finger-measures of the arm-lines, it is known as the *iṣṭaprabhā*.
3.06a: A line situated from east to west is called the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍala);
3.06b: and it is also proclaimed as the meridian circle (viṣuvanmaṇḍala) on the celestial sphere.
3.07a: A line should be drawn from east to west, as well as one extending to the tip of the equinoctial shadow.
3.07b: The distance between the desired shadow and the equinoctial shadow is called the *agrā*.
The square root of the sum of the square of the gnomon and the square of the shadow is the hypotenuse;
from the square of this [hypotenuse], subtracting the square of the gnomon, the square root is the shadow, and conversely, the gnomon.

3.09a: Thirty times during a yuga, the wheel of the lunar mansions (bhānām cakraṃ) revolves eastward. 3.09b: When the number of days of the yuga (dyugaṇa) is divided by that [number] multiplied by the number of terrestrial days (bhūdina), the result obtained is...

3.10a: Those degrees multiplied by three and divided by ten are to be known as the precession (ayanāṃśa). 3.10b: From the planet corrected by that [precession], [one calculates] the declination, shadow, half-day-arc, and so forth.
3.11a: Clearly, the equality of observation occurs during the two solstices and the two equinoxes.
3.11b: The circle has shifted eastward when the shadow is less than that derived from the astronomical manual.
3.12a: Then, having subtracted the intermediate parts, [one proceeds] with the remaining [parts] when there is an excess;
3.12b: thus is the equinoctial shadow produced at midday in one's own location.
3.13a: On the north-south line, that is the equinoctial shadow there.
3.13b: The two [sine] values of the trijyā (radius), multiplied by the gnomon-shadow and divided by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow, yield the sines of the colatitude and the latitude.
3.14a: The arcs of these two are always the southern colatitude and latitude.
3.14b: The midday shadow is the base; the circumference of the triad (the radius) is multiplied by that.
The degrees of the bow subtracted from their own ears are the south declinations;
those in the north are the north declinations, which are the minutes of the sun's transverse motion (sūryakrānti).
3.16a: When there is a difference in direction, the arc-minutes are combined; when they are equal, they are subtracted.

From those [arc-minutes], the sine of the arc is obtained, and having subtracted its square from the square of the radius, the square root [is taken]. 3.16b: [The result is] the cosine of the arc; and having subtracted its square from the square of the radius, the square root [is taken].
3.17a: The equinoctial shadow is obtained by multiplying the latitude (akṣajyā) by the sine of the colatitude (lambajyā) and dividing by the sine of the sun's altitude (arkaguṇa).

3.17b: The difference between the degrees of the sun's altitude and the degrees of the zenith distance (natabhāga) is taken according to their direction; if they are of the same direction, it is the difference, otherwise it is the sum.
3.18a: When there is a difference in direction, the remainder is the declination; its sine, multiplied by the radius and divided by the maximum sine of declination, [yields the arc].
3.18b: The Sun is in Aries and so forth when the resulting arc is positive.
3.19: Having subtracted [the longitude] from half the circle starting from Cancer, and having added half the circle starting from Libra;
and having subtracted it from the full circle starting from Capricorn—at midday, the Sun becomes thus corrected (sphuṭa).
3.20a: That [latitude] is slow; when it is repeatedly to the left, the result is middling, and the sun is at midday.
3.20b: The sum of the sines of the latitude and the sun's declination is the direction when they are of opposite signs; otherwise, it is the difference.

3.21a: The remainder is the sun’s degrees of altitude (natāṃśāḥ), and their sine and cosine are the bāhu-jyā and koṭi-jyā respectively. 3.21b: These [sines] are multiplied by the measure of the gnomon in finger-breadths, according to their respective order, to obtain the bhuja and trijyā.
3.22a: Divided by the cotangent (koṭijyā), the results obtained are the shadow (chāyā) and the hypotenuse (karṇa) at midday.
3.22b: The sine of declination (krāntijyā), multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse (viṣuvatkarṇa) and divided by the sine of the gnomon-shadow (śaṅkujīvā), [is the result].
3.23a: The tip of the sun's shadow, multiplied by its own hypotenuse and divided by the middle hypotenuse, is its own [corrected] value.
3.23b: When added to the equinoctial shadow, it becomes the northern arm (bhuja) if the sun is in the southern hemisphere.
3.24a: At the equinox, having subtracted [the latitude] from the northern hemisphere, the northward arm (bāhu) shall be obtained.
3.24b: By the reverse process, the southward arm (bhuja) becomes the interval between east and west.
3.25a: The midday shadow is always known as the midday shadow (mādhyāhnikī-chāyā).
3.25b: The sine of the latitude and the sine of the colatitude are multiplied by twelve and by the equinoctial shadow, respectively.
3.26a: When the Sun is situated on the equatorial circle, those two ears (the hypotenuses) are obtained from the latitude-chord (krāntijyā).
3.26b: When the declination is diminished by the northern latitude, then it is the hypotenuse of the half-day.

3.27a: The karṇa multiplied by the midday shadow and divided by the difference between the midday shadow and the tip [of the gnomon] is the sine of its own declination. 3.27b: Multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the colatitude, it is the cord of the tip.

3.28a: The *agrā* (shadow-tip) in digits and so forth is obtained by multiplying the sine of the desired [latitude] by the radius (*karṇa*) and dividing by the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyā*).
3.28b: From the square of the *agrājyā* subtracted from half the square of the radius and multiplied by twelve; //
3.29a: Furthermore, whatever result is obtained by the wise from [the square of the shadow] multiplied by twelve;
3.29b: [That result is derived] from the square of the equinoctial shadow increased by half the square of the gnomon, and divided [by that same sum].
3.30a: That very [value] is called the *karaṇī*; the wise man should set it aside separately.
3.30b: It is likewise multiplied by the equinoctial shadow multiplied by the sine of the [latitude] from the tip of the shadow.
3.31a: The square root of that [quantity] combined with its group, divided by the result;
3.31b: [This] is diminished by or added to the result, respectively, for the southern and northern hemispheres.

When the sun is in the south, the gnomon revolves in the two intermediate directions of the south; likewise, when the sun is in the north, that gnomon revolves in the two intermediate directions of the north.

3.33a: The square root of the difference between the squares of those two [sines] is called the *dṛgjyā* (versed sine). 3.33b: Dividing [the *dṛgjyā*] by its own *śaṅku* (shadow), one obtains the *dṛk* and *trijyā* (versed and full sines) multiplied by twelve.

3.34a: At the corners, the shadow-ears (chāyākarṇau) are according to their respective places and times; 3.34b: In the northern [hemisphere], they are increased by the sine of the ascensional difference (udakcarajā); in the southern, they are decreased by that.
3.35a: The last [sine] increased by its own versed sine and decreased by the versed sine of the [latitude] arc, multiplied by half the local day-and-night period (svahorātrārdha), 3.35b:
and divided by the radius (trijyā), shall be the divisor; then, multiplied by the sine of the colatitude (lambajyā) and divided [by the same radius], it becomes the [result].
The gnomon shall be obtained by dividing [the radius] by the sine of the latitude; one should subtract its square from the square of the radius of the celestial sphere.
The square root of that remainder is the sine of the altitude; the shadow and the hypotenuse are as previously described.

3.37a: The sine of the zenith distance (*dṛgjyā*) is the sine of the maximum altitude (*trijyā*) multiplied by the desired shadow and divided by its hypotenuse (*karṇa*). 3.37b–3.8a: The square root of the difference between the square of the sine of the maximum altitude and the square of that [sine of the zenith distance] is the gnomon (*śaṅku*). That [gnomon], multiplied by the sine of the maximum altitude (*tribhajīvā*) and divided by the sine of the local latitude (*svalambajyā*), [is the desired shadow].
3.38b: That [arc] multiplied by the radius and divided by half the equinoctial day [of that latitude] is the [sine of the] amplitude.
3.39a: The arc of the remainder is the difference between the last [sine] and that [sine] diminished by the corresponding versed sine (unnatajyā).
3.39b: In this manner, the *prāk* and *paścāt* half-depressions (*natāsava*) are obtained through the versed sines (*utkramajyā*).

3.40a: But the lambajyā multiplied by the desired sine and divided by its own radius (svakarṇa) [is the result]; 3.40b: that is the krāntijyā (sine of declination), which, when multiplied by the trijīvā (radius of the celestial sphere) and divided by the maximum apakrama (maximum sine of declination), [yields the desired value].

3.41a: That field beginning with the sign [occupied by] the bow (the ninth house) is the domain; the Sun situated therein, on the desired day, at midday, or before or after, within a distance of three armspans, [is the point]. 3.41b: [The Sun] is held [there] in the middle, whether in front or behind.
3.42a: When the two fish [of the sine] are joined by the interval, there is the revolution of light by means of the three-pointed cord (trispṛk-sūtra).
3.42b: The [sines] multiplied by half the radius and divided by half the equatorial day-night period (svāhorātra) [are the sines of the ascensional differences].

3.43a: The sines of one, two, and three [units] respectively are divided by those [sines], and their respective arcs are subtracted one after another from below; then, from Aries, the *laṅkodaya* (ascensional differences) in *nāḍī*-seconds are obtained.
3.44a: Thirty-eight, forty-six, forty-one, forty-nine, thirty-three, thirty-seven, and thirty-two;
3.44b: These, diminished by the degrees traversed in one's own country, become the desired rising-seconds (iṣṭodayāsavaḥ).
3.45a: The three signs beginning with Cancer, when added respectively to their own [corresponding] scattered [components], 3.45b:
these same six, in reverse order, become the desired signs beginning with Libra.
3.46a: The elapsed and remaining *āsava*s should be calculated from the Sun at the desired time.
3.46b: Multiplied by their respective *udaya-āsava*s and divided by thirty (khavahni), they become the elapsed and remaining [degrees].
3.47a: One should subtract the elapsed *asūs* from the desired *ghaṭikās* and *asūs*;
3.47b: likewise, one should subtract the future *asūs* of that [ascendant] from the future *asūs* of the ascendant; and similarly, one should subtract them in reverse order from the elapsed [time].
3.48a: If the remainder is multiplied by thirty and divided by the [ascendant] divisor, 3.48b:
and then added to or subtracted from the degrees, that is the ascendant at the horizon at that time.
3.49ab: From that [meridian distance], having subtracted or added the nāḍīs of prior or posterior natation by means of the Laṅkā-rising times,
the midheaven (madhyalagna) is then obtained when the sun is in decrease or increase [of day].

Then, having added together the remaining breaths (*bhogyāsūn*) of the lesser [longitude] and the elapsed breaths (*bhuktāsūn*) of the greater, as well as the breaths corresponding to the interval between them, this shall be the calculation of time (*kālasādhana*).
3.51a: When the sun is less [than the ascendant], it is the remainder of the night; when the ascendant is greater than the sun, it is by day.
3.51b: When the sun is greater than the sun plus half the zodiacal circle (bhacakrārdha), it is after sunset.
The diameter of the solar orb is six thousand five hundred yojanas;
that of the lunar orb is four hundred and eighty.
4.02a: Multiplied by the true velocity and divided by the mean velocity, they become true.
4.02b: [The result] for the Sun is multiplied by its own revolutions and divided by the Moon's revolutions.
4.03a: Multiplied by the circumference of the moon’s orbit, or divided by the circumference of the sun’s orbit;
4.03b: this is the diameter at the moon’s orbit; the measure in minutes [of arc] is obtained by dividing that by the number of lunar days (tithis).

4.04a: The true motion of the moon, multiplied by the diameter of the earth and divided by the mean [motion], 4.04b: yields the needle; it is the difference between the diameter of the earth and the true hypotenuse of the sun.
4.05a: Multiplied by the diameter of the middle moon and divided by the diameter of the middle sun; 4.05b:
subtracting the quotient from the needle [radius], the resulting minutes of arc are the measure of the shadow, as before.
4.06a: When the shadow of the earth is equal to half the diameter of the sun, and when the moon’s node is likewise equal to the sun;
4.06b: there is an eclipse, provided the node is less by some number of degrees.

4.07a: At the time of the end of the new moon, the sun and the moon shall be equal in terms of their signs and other divisions. 4.07b: At the end of the full moon, they are equal in degrees and so forth when [the moon] is at half the zodiac (bhārdha).
The two [nodes] become equal in minutes when [the true anomaly] is diminished or increased by the respective fruit of the past and future parvan-nāḍīs;
otherwise, it is the instantaneous node.
4.09a: The moon, situated below the sun, becomes like a cloud that obscures it;
4.09b: Facing eastward, the moon enters the shadow of the earth, and thus it becomes [an eclipse].

4.10: Having subtracted the instantaneous latitude of the moon from half the sum of the measures of the eclipsed and the eclipsing bodies, that which remains is called the measure of the obscured portion.
4.11a: When that [longitude] is greater than the [longitude of the] eclipsed body, the total eclipse occurs; otherwise, it is partial.
4.11b: If the latitude (vikṣepa) is greater than half the sum [of the diameters], the occurrence of an eclipse is impossible.
4.12a: The conjunctions and disjunctions of the "grasped" (grāhya) and the "grasper" (grāhaka) are separately eliminated.
4.12b: From those two squares, diminished by the square of the [respective] displacements (vikṣepa), both square roots are obtained.

4.13a: Having multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference between the motions of the sun and the moon, 4.13b: there shall be the results in nāḍīs and so forth for the half-duration and the half-eclipse of those two.
4.14a: The velocities multiplied by the *nāḍikās* of the half-duration and divided by sixty [yield] minutes of arc (*liptā*) and so forth;
these are to be subtracted at the first contact (*pragraha*) and added again and again at the release (*mokṣa*).

4.15a: By means of its [the anomaly's] corrections, the half-arc of the station (sthitidala) and likewise the half-arc of the submergence (vimardārdha) should be repeatedly calculated; otherwise, that result in minutes and so forth would belong to the node (pāta).
4.15b: Otherwise, that result in minutes and so forth would belong to the node (pāta).
4.16a: One should indicate the middle of the eclipse at the conclusion of the clearly determined lunar day;
4.16b: the immersion occurs when the duration is diminished by the half-duration in nāḍīs, while the emergence occurs when it is added.
In exactly the same way, when [the duration] is increased by half a nāḍī less than the *vimarda*,
there occur the two [phases] called *nimīlana* (closing) and *unmīlana* (opening) during a total eclipse.
4.18a–b: One should multiply the difference in the velocities of the sun and the moon by the duration of the station diminished by the elapsed nāḍīs;
the result divided by sixty gives the *koṭiliptās*.
4.19a: When there is an eclipse of the Sun, the koti-seconds multiplied by the mean duration of the eclipse, 4.19b:
and divided by the true duration of the eclipse, are known as the true koti-seconds.
The difference between those two is the base (bhuja); the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse (śrava).
Having subtracted this from half the sum of the diameters, the resulting value shall be the instantaneous measure of the eclipse (grāsa).
4.21a: From the moment of mid-eclipse, one should subtract the desired nāḍīs;
4.21b: from the duration of liberation (maukṣika-sthityardha), the remainder is as before, but the remainder is [calculated] for the liberation phase.
4.22a: From half the sum of the longitudes of the planet and its apogee, subtract the degrees of its own anomaly;
4.22b: having subtracted from the square of that result the square of the equation of center for that time, take the square root.
4.23a: The *koṭiliptās* multiplied by the true half-duration (*spaṣṭasthityardha*) of the Sun and divided by its mean [half-duration];
4.23b: the resulting *liptās* are the *nāḍīs*, and the *grāsanāḍikās* are like the duration (*sthiti*).
4.24a: The sine of the latitude multiplied by the natural sine of the altitude and divided by the radius gives its arc.
4.24b: These are the degrees of deflection, north or south, in the eastern and western hemispheres respectively.
4.25a: From the quantity to be taken (grāhya) increased by three signs, [the degrees] added to the north-south declination degrees;
4.25b: in the case of difference, the arc between them is the *valana* (deflection), divided by seventy finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
4.26a: One should divide the sun's depression by half of the midday [shadow] and then multiply it by the result of the half-day [shadow].
4.26b: One should divide the measures of the [planetary] latitudes by those [values]; these are their values in finger-breadths (aṅgula).

5.01a: When the sun is equal to the meridian ascendant, there is no possibility of *harija*. 5.01b: When the declination of the sun is equal to the product of the latitude and the sine of the meridian zenith distance, there is also no *avanati*.
5.02a: Just as the occurrence of parallax is according to the specific place and time, 5.02b: so too it is stated [to occur] due to the east and other directions.

5.03a: One should calculate the ascendant from the nadīs at the end of the lunar node by means of their own rising-seconds (udayāsus). 5.03b: Its sine, multiplied by the sine of the maximum declination and divided by the sine of the colatitude, is called the "rising-sine" (udayajyā).
5.04a: Then, the ascendant at the rising of Laṅkā is designated as the "midpoint" (madhya) as previously described.
5.04b: The sum of its [the midday point's] declination and the latitude is [the oblique ascension]; if they are of opposite directions, it is their difference.
The remainder is the angle of depression; its sine is called the middle chord (madhyajyā).
Multiplied by the sine of the meridian altitude and divided by the radius, the square of that result [is obtained].

5.06a: The hypotenuse (dṛkkṣepa) is the square root of the difference between the square of the mid-arc sine and [the square of] the [given] sine; 5.06b: the gnomon (śaṅku) is the square root of the difference between the square of that [hypotenuse] and the square of the radius (trijyā); that is the visual motion (dṛggati).
The sines of the nadir and the cosine of the arm are the uncorrected parallax in latitude and the parallax in longitude;
the divisor is obtained by taking one half of a sine, and the quotient is found by means of the sine of the parallax in longitude.
5.08a: The sine of the difference between the midheaven and the sun, divided by the divisor (cheda), 5.08b:
should be known as the parallax (lambana) of the sun and moon, expressed in ghaṭīs and so forth, occurring either before or after [the true time].
5.09a: When the sun is greater than the midheaven, one should subtract [the result] from the end of the lunar day (tithi).
5.09b: When it is less, [the result] is positive; this process is repeated repeatedly until everything becomes stable.

5.10a: The parallax of the Moon and the Sun, multiplied by the difference between their mean motions, 5.10b: and divided by the product of the number of lunar days and the radius, shall be the resulting correction for civil time (sāvana).
5.11a: From the displacement of the observer (dṛkkṣepa), divided by seventy, the result shall be the depression (avanati).
5.11b: Or else, from [the displacement] multiplied by forty-nine and divided by the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā).
5.12a: And that [latitude] is to be understood as south or north according to the direction of the mid-heaven (madhyajyā) and so forth;
5.12b: it is added when the direction of the moon's [orbital] deviation (vikṣepa) is the same, and subtracted otherwise.
5.13a: By that [method], the duration of stay, the eclipse, the half-eclipse, and so forth are as previously stated;
5.13b: the magnitude, the deflection, the desired extent of the eclipse, and so on, are like those of the moon.
5.14a: From the [longitude] increased or decreased by half the duration of the station, as before, the parallax at the end of the lunar day (tithi) is again calculated.
5.14b: That which arises from the commencement and release of the eclipse must be determined; it is the difference between that and the mid-eclipse [longitude] produced by the sun.
5.15a: If the eastern observation occurs before the meridian, the parallax for the eastern hemisphere would be greater than that for the middle;
5.15b: the parallax for the western hemisphere is less, but the reverse is true for the latter half.
5.16a: Then, during the period of liberation and stability, as well as during the period of grasping, [the correction] should be applied;
5.16b: the difference between the [mean] sun and [true] sun is to be subtracted wherever this reversal occurs.
5.17a: This has been stated regarding the unity of the [lunar] hemisphere; when there is a difference between them, there is unity of the *lambana*.
5.17b: It should be added to each respective portion of the stay (*sthitidalaka*), and likewise to half of the *vimarda*, as previously described.
[Chedyaka] 6.01a: Since distinct types of apprehension are not clearly known apart from the *chedyaka*, 6.01b:
I shall therefore explain that supreme knowledge of the *chedyaka*.
6.02a: Having well-prepared the ground and marked a central point, one should then draw the mandala based on its curvature, starting with a radius of seven finger-breadths.
6.02b: [One should first draw] the mandala resting upon the curved lines, using a measurement of seven finger-breadths from the initial point.
The second mandala is measured by half the sum of the object of perception and the perceiver; that third [mandala], known as the "abbreviated," is measured by half the object of perception.
6.04a: The determination of the directions—south, north, east, and west—is as before.
6.04b: For the moon, the eclipse occurs first and the release later; for the sun, it is the reverse.
6.05a: Prior to its apprehension, the deflection of the moon is according to the direction [of its motion]; 6.05b: but that of the planet Mercury is reversed; this is the opposite for the sun.
6.06a: If the thread should touch the middle from the tip of the curve, then, upon its intersection, the two deviations—the swallowing and the releasing—should be applied.
6.06b: [The same applies] when it is equal; thus the two deviations, characterized by swallowing and release, are to be given.
6.07a: Again, one should insert the thread from the tip of the projection into the central point.
6.07b: From the contact with that point to be grasped, one should indicate the swallowing and the release.
6.08a: The daily latitudes of the Sun in the parilekha are as directed [in the table].
6.08b: Those of the Moon are the reverse; then, by virtue of that, the mean [longitude] is determined.
6.09a: If there is unity between that [latitude] and its declination, a correction toward the east should be applied;
6.09b: in the case of a difference, it should be applied toward the west for the moon, and the reverse for the sun.
6.10a: Again, one should lead the thread from the tip of the *valana* to the central point.
6.10b: By means of the central thread, one should direct the deviation toward the *valana*.

6.11a: From the tip of the displacement, one should draw a circle with a radius equal to the semi-diameter of the eclipsing body; 6.11b: that portion of the circle of the eclipsed body which is intersected by it becomes obscured by darkness.

6.12a: While drawing a diagram on the ground or on a board, the wise man should perform the reversal of the directions for the eastern and western hemispheres. 6.12b: [The reversal of the directions for the eastern and western hemispheres should be performed.]
6.13a: Because of its clarity, even a twelfth part of the moon that is eclipsed is visible; 6.13b: But because of its sharpness, not even three *liptās* of the sun that are eclipsed are seen.
6.14a: Three dots designated as "one's own" (svasaṃjñita) should be placed at the tips of the [three] divergences;
6.14b: there, between the eastern and middle [divergences], and likewise between the middle and the one pertaining to liberation (maukṣika).
6.15a: One should draw two fish [diagrams] from between those two, extending from mouth to tail. 6.15b: Having stretched out two threads, one should mark the point where their intersection occurs.
6.16a: There, one should draw an arc with a cord that touches three points;
6.16b: that is said to be the path by which the perceiver will proceed.

6.17a: Having subtracted from the half-sum of the conjunction of the eclipsed and the eclipsing [bodies] the eclipse obtained as the maximum; 6.17b: one should draw a rod equal in length to the remaining finger-breadths from the central point.
6.18a: To those two, one should give [the offering] facing the path of the *grāhya*, first directed toward the *grāhaka*.
6.18b: As he releases it toward the direction of liberation, she indeed follows the path of the *grāhaka*.
6.19a: Wherever [the shadow] touches, one should then draw a circle with half the diameter of the object.
6.19b: That part of the object which is covered by that [circle] should be declared as eclipsed by Rāhu.

One should insert a probe called *nimīlana*, measured by half the length of the instrument, pointing toward the direction of the bolus; it should be applied such that it touches the path where [the stone] lies.
6.21a: Then, with the segment of the grāhaka [circle], one should draw the mandala as before.
6.21b: Wherever there is a conjunction of that [segment] with the grāhya-maṇḍala, there is the closing (nimīlana).
6.22a: Thus, upon opening [the eyes], one should extend [the gaze] toward the direction of liberation;
6.22b: one should draw the mandala as before, and then perform the opening as previously described.
6.23a: When less than half [of the sun's orb] is eclipsed, it should be smoky; when more than half, it becomes black.
6.23b: During a total eclipse, the solar disc releases its blackness and becomes tawny (kapila).
6.24a: This secret of the gods must not be given to just anyone;
6.24b: It should be given to a well-tested disciple who has resided [with the teacher] for a year.
[Planetary Conjunction] 7.01a: Among the luminous planets, there shall be mutual conflict and conjunction;
7.01b: conjunction with the Moon, and setting together with the Sun.

7.02a: When the slower planet is exceeded by the faster one, the conjunction has already occurred; otherwise, it will occur in the future. 7.02b: This applies when both are moving forward; however, for those in retrograde motion, the reverse is true.
7.03a: When the planet moving forward (prāgyāyin) is greater [than the other], the conjunction has passed; when it is retrograde (vakrin), the conjunction is yet to come.
7.03b: The degrees of difference between the two planets are multiplied by their respective minutes of daily motion.
7.04a: One should divide by the difference in motion for both direct and retrograde [planets];
7.04b: but when one is retrograde, one should divide by the sum of their motions.
7.05a: The obtained value in minutes and so forth should be subtracted from the elapsed [longitude] and added to the future [longitude].
7.05b: In the case of retrograde motion, this is reversed; however, when both are retrograde, there is addition and subtraction [respectively].
7.06a: Those two planets, situated within their respective zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa), shall be [calculated as] smeared together;
7.06b: having likewise subtracted that difference, the result in days and so forth is desired.

7.07a: Having calculated the length of day and night, as well as the minutes of ascensional difference (vikṣepaliptikāḥ), 7.07b: one should determine the degrees of depression and elevation (natonnata) for those two [the sun and the moon] from their respective times according to the ascendant (lagna).

7.08a: From the shadow at the equinox, subtracted by its declination and divided by twelve; 7.08b: the result, multiplied by the nāḍīs of one's own nativity and divided by half of one's own day, [is the desired value].

7.09a: A debt is obtained from the east; from the north-western displacement, there is wealth in the west. 7.09b: In the southern eastern hemisphere, there is one's own property; likewise, in the western [hemisphere], there is loss.
7.10a: The seconds of the additive (kṣepaliptikā) are multiplied by the degrees of the obliquity (krānti) derived from the planet with its [precession] correction.
7.10b: These are the seconds; they are positive or negative according to whether the obliquity and the additive are of different or the same sign, respectively.

7.11a: In the conjunctions of lunar mansions and planets, in calculating the heliacal rising and setting of planets, and 7.11b: in the case of the moon’s horn-illumination (śṛṅgonnati), this [method] is prescribed for the calculation of parallax (dṛkkarma) and other such matters.
7.12a: Furthermore, the two displacements (vikṣepas) for those two must then be calculated for that specific time.
7.12b: If they are in the same direction, the difference [between them] is taken; if they differ in direction, their sum is the remaining distance between the planets.
7.13a: In the orbit of the Moon, the Viṣkambha [distances] for Mars, Saturn, Mercury, and Jupiter are increased by half and half of thirty [respectively].
7.13b: For Venus, sixty is stated.

7.14a: Multiplied by three and four respectively, divided by the sine of the amplitude (karṇa), and doubled, these [values] multiplied by the radius (trijyā) [yield the results]. 7.14b: These are the true sines of their respective amplitudes; when divided by fifteen (tithi), they become the minutes of arc for the [planetary] diameters.
7.15a: When the shadow-ground is inverted, one should show the planet at the tip of its own shadow;
7.15b: the planet situated within its own mirror is indicated at the tip of the gnomon.

7.16a: Two stakes, five cubits high, are positioned according to the directions for the purpose of rotation; 7.16b: they are suspended by a cord from the planets and fixed in the ground at a depth of one cubit below.
7.17a: Then one should draw two shadow-ears from the tip of the shadow to the top of the gnomon;
7.17b: one should demonstrate [the point] situated at the junction of the tips of the two shadow-ears.

When two planets in the sky have their gnomon-roots meeting at the zenith and have attained equality in their visual arc, there is the *ullekha* (piercing) conjunction due to the touching of their stars; when there is a difference [in their positions], that is proclaimed as *bheda* (separation).
7.19a: A battle known as *aṃśuvimarda* occurs when there is a mutual conjunction of degrees (*aṃśu*).
7.19b: If [the degrees] are less than a degree (*aṃśa*), the battle is called *apasavya*, provided that one of them is a minute (*aṇu*) [planet].
7.20a: If the conjunction occurs when [the Moon] is more than half [full] and both [planets] are endowed with strength;
7.20b: [then] in a battle, one situated on the left is victorious, while the small planet is eclipsed and rendered lusterless.
7.21a: Rūkṣa (rough), vivarṇa (discolored), vidhvasta (ruined), and vijita (conquered) [are the results] when [the moon] is situated in the south (dakṣiṇāśrita).
7.21b: Udakṣtha (upward-facing), dīptimān (radiant), sthūla (stout), and jayin (victorious) [are the results] even when it is powerful in the south.
7.22a: Even if both are close and blazing, if there is a conjunction; 7.22b:
even if both are small and eclipsed, they may form a deceptive configuration.
7.23a: A descendant of Bhṛgu situated in the north or the south is generally victorious.
7.23b: In this same manner, one should determine the conjunctions of these [planets] with the Moon.

7.24a: This conceptual construction has been presented for the sake of explaining the existence and non-existence of the worlds; 7.24b: yet these [beings], relying upon one another, proceed far from their own true path.

The minutes of arc for the conjunctions of the lunar mansions and planets are declared; then, one's own portion multiplied by ten becomes the constant (dhruva) added to the minutes of arc traversed by the past mansions.
8.02a: Sixty-five [and] sixty-seven, with eight oceans [and] made void;
8.02b: Eight objects, four oceans, eight-legged, legless limbs, and likewise Manus.
Eight, three, and five; four, six, and zero; zero, five, and zero;
zero, four, and seven; seven, seven, and eight; seven, four, and six.
8.04a: Then the *manava* [nakṣatra] is in *rasā*; the *vaiśva* [nakṣatra] extends halfway through *āpya*.
8.04b: At the end of *āpya* itself is *abhijit*; at the end of *vaiśva* is the position of *śravaṇa*. 8.05a: *Śraviṣṭhā* is at the junction of the third and fourth quarters of *śravaṇa*.
8.05b: From one's own enjoyment, the nāgas are thirty-two; six, twenty-four, and thirty.

8.06a: Their equations of the center (vikṣepas) are nine, eight, and six degrees respectively from their own apogees; 8.06b: they are positive in the northern [latitude] and negative in the southern, being five, ten, and nine degrees [respectively].
8.07a: In the north, [the degrees] are six and zero; in the south, seven; in the north, thirty-six;
thirteen in the south; 8.07b: eleven in the south, and thirty-seven in the north.
In the southern direction, there are nine, one and a half, three, and forty-five;
likewise in the northern direction, there are sixty, thirty, and thirty-six.
8.09a: On the right side, however, there is a half-part [plus] twenty-four;
on the left, twenty-six parts and zero, for the Aśvinīs and the others in their respective order.
8.10a: Agastya is situated at eighty degrees in the southern [hemisphere], at the end of Gemini; 8.10b: and Mṛgavyādha is established at the twentieth degree of Gemini.
8.11a: The displacement [of the sun] from its own obliquity is to the south by four hundred and sixty degrees.
8.11b: In Taurus, the fire-god (Aries) and the heart of Brahma (Capricorn) are situated at twenty-two degrees.
8.12a: By thirty-eight and thirty [degrees] respectively, those two are displaced to the north;
8.12b: having obtained the *gola*, one should examine the displacement and the precise *dhruvaka*.
8.13a: When the southern declination of a star exceeds two degrees in the seventeenth division of the asterism Vṛṣa (Taurus), 8.13b: it shall pierce the cart of Rohiṇī.

8.14a: One should perform the correction for latitude (dṛkkarma) as before, using the light of the planets during day and night like [the method for] a planet. 8.14b: The remainder and the number of days are calculated by means of the planetary motion, just as in the conjunction of planets.

8.15a: When the planet is moving forward (eṣya), the conjunction occurs when it is below the *dhruvaka*; when it is above, it occurs from that [point]. 8.15b: In the case of a retrograde planet (*vakragata*), the encounter should be understood through the reverse [calculation].
8.16a: Likewise, for the two Phālgunas, the two Bhādrapadas, and the two Āṣāḍhas;
8.16b: Viśākhā, Aśvinī, and Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) are recorded as having the Uttarā stars as their junction-stars.
The second star from the western-northern star is situated in the west;
it is the junction-star of Hasta and is also the westernmost star of Śraviṣṭhā.
8.18a: For Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, and Maitra, the midday [oblation] belongs to Bṛhaspati;
8.18b: for Bharaṇī, Āgneya, Pitrya, and Revatī, the oblation is in the afternoon.
8.19a: The eastern direction belongs to Rohiṇī, Āditya (Punarvasu), Mūla, and Sārpa (Āśleṣā). 8.19b:
For all the remaining [asterisms], the yoga-tārakā (the junction star) should be understood as being toward the north.
In the east, Prajāpati is situated five degrees from the Brahmahṛdaya;
he is at the end of the Bull (Vṛṣa) in the north at thirty-eight degrees.
8.21a: But the Apām-vatsa [constellation] is five degrees to the north of Citrā;
8.21b: Bṛhat is slightly further from that, and likewise Āpaḥ is six degrees to the north.
9.01a: Now, the thorough knowledge of rising and setting is proclaimed;
9.01b: concerning those whose forms are overtaken by the rays of the sun and whose brilliance has faded.
9.02a: Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn set after the sun;
9.02b: Venus and Mercury, as well as those in retrograde motion, rise before it when they are less [in longitude].
9.03a: When Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are less than Vivasvat [the Sun] in the east, they set;
9.03b: when they are greater, they rise in the west, owing to their swifter motion.

One should perform the correction for parallax (*dṛkkarma*) on the sun and planets during the day: for those west of the meridian at sunset, using their positions at sunset; and for those east of the meridian at sunrise, using their positions at sunrise. Then, one should apply the parallax correction to the planet.
9.05a: Then, the breaths (asus) of the interval between the ascendants, divided by sixty, are the *kālāṃśas*.
9.05b: In the case of the western [hemisphere], when the two are added to six signs, the breaths of the interval between the ascendants are likewise [calculated].
9.06a: Eleven degrees belong to Jupiter, and those of Saturn are equal to the number of lunar days (fifteen).
9.06b: Those of Mars are eighteen degrees, and thereafter, ten degrees more than seven (seventeen) [belong to Rahu].

9.07a: Sunset occurs in the west by eight [degrees], and sunrise in the east due to its greater magnitude; 9.07b: for Venus (Bhṛgu), sunset is in the east and sunrise in the west due to its lesser magnitude, by ten [degrees].
Thus, when retrograde by twelve or fourteen degrees from the Sun, the wise [planet] causes its heliacal setting and rising; and when moving with swift motion, it likewise does so.
9.09: Due to these additional portions of time, the sky-dwellers become visible in the world; when [the portions] are deficient, they remain unseen, their forms eclipsed by the rays of the sun.
The degrees of difference between the two [mean] times, converted to minutes, divided by the difference in their velocities, yield the result in days and so forth;
for a retrograde planet, this result is obtained by dividing by the sum of the velocities.
The portions traversed [by the planets] multiplied by the ascendant and the life-span, and divided by one thousand eight hundred, shall be the time and motion;
from these two, the elapsed and remaining days and so forth are determined.
9.12a: Svāti, Agastya (Canopus), Mṛgavyādha (Mṛgaśīrṣa), Citrā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Punarvasu;
9.12b: along with Abhijit, known as Brahmahṛdaya, [are situated] at thirteen degrees [from the beginning of the asterism].
9.13a: Hasta, Śravaṇa, the two Phālgunīs, Śraviṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, and Maghā;
9.13b: Viśākhā and the constellation presided over by Aśvin are visible for fourteen degrees.
9.14a: Kṛttikā, Anurādhā, Mūla, Āśleṣā, and also the asterism of Rudra (Ārdrā);
9.14b: these are seen for fifteen days, as are the two [asterisms] following Āṣāḍhā.
9.15a: Bharaṇī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), and Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) are visible for three and seven parts (21 degrees) due to their subtlety;
9.15b: the remaining stars are visible for seventeen parts, while others are invisible.

The degrees visible [above the horizon] multiplied by one thousand eight hundred and divided by the right ascensions of their respective risings yield the degrees of the arc; or else, by means of those [degrees], the visibility or invisibility [of the planet] is determined.
9.17a: Their rising is before [the meridian] and their setting is after; the correction for visibility (*dṛkkarma*) is as previously described.
9.17b: For the attainment of the elapsed or future day is always determined by the motion of the sun.
9.18a: Abhijit, Brahmahṛdaya, Svāti, Vaiṣṇava, and Vāsava;
9.18b: and Ahirbudhnya, because they are situated in the north, are not eclipsed by the rays of the sun.

The procedure for the rising and setting of the moon should be performed as previously described. It becomes visible in the west after twelve degrees [of elongation], and it goes out of sight in the east.
10.02a: From the sum of the Sun and the Moon increased by six signs, the *ghatis* of the interval from the ascendant are calculated as before.
10.02b: When the Sun and the Moon are in the same sign, the minutes of arc of their difference must be calculated.
10.03a: Those [mean] motions of the sun and the moon, multiplied by the elapsed nāḍīs and divided by sixty, yield the results;
10.03b: the difference in degrees (asus) should then be calculated again for the two [mean planets] increased by those results.

10.04a: In this manner, until the *āsavas* (units of time) between the sun and the moon have become fixed; 10.04b: by those *prāṇas*, the moon sets after the sunset of the sun during the bright fortnight (*śukla*).
10.05a: Having added half a lunar mansion (bhagaṇārdha) to the sun, the remaining degrees (asavaḥ) should be calculated;
by those breaths (prāṇas), the moon reaches its rising during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).

10.06a: The difference of the longitudinal displacements (krānti) of the Sun and Moon is the declination when they are in opposite directions; otherwise, it is their sum. 10.06b: The sine of that [arc] is the latitude of the Moon from the Sun; where this [latitude] is, it should be known as south or north.
10.07a: If that [latitude] is north and multiplied by the sine of the meridian zenith distance of the midday moon;
10.07b: then it should be subtracted from the sine of the observer's latitude multiplied by the sun's [sine of altitude], or added if it is south.
The remainder, divided by the lambajyā (sine of the colatitude), yields the bāhu (base), which faces its own direction;
the koṭi (perpendicular) is the gnomon (śaṅku). The square root of the sum of the squares of these two shall be the śruti (hypotenuse).
10.09a: The minutes of arc of the Sun minus those of the Moon, divided by nine hundred, [give the result];
10.09b: multiplied by the digits of the Moon’s disc and divided by twelve, it is the true [ecliptic limit].
10.10a: Having placed the dot known as the sun (arka), one should then [place] the arm facing its own direction;
10.10b: then the tip [of the arm] facing west, and the ear situated between the tip and the middle.
10.11a: From the point joined with the tip of the radius, one should draw the instantaneous disk.
10.11b: By means of the radius-line, one should first determine the cardinal directions.

10.12a: One should lead that white [line] inward toward the center by means of the ear (the intersection), due to its connection with the circle. 10.12b: One should establish two fish-marks between the southern and northern tips of the white line.
10.13a: From the conjunction of the thread passing through the center of that [circle], one should draw a bow [shape] touching the three points.
10.13b: On that day, the moon shall appear exactly as its eastern reflection.
10.14a: Because the direction is established by the tip [of the thread], one should show the raised horn among the animals at the end of the cord.
10.14b: Having made the form of the moon, one should display the raised tip.
10.15a: Having subtracted the sun increased by six from Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the dark [portion] from the moon; 10.15b: one should place the left arm there; that is the western mandala of the moon.
When the sun and the moon are on the same path and their orbs are joined, such that their declinations are equal, it is called *vaidhṛta*.
When the Moon and the Sun have entered opposite courses, the sum of their longitudinal minutes of arc is then Vyatīpāta; this occurs when the two are joined at half a zodiacal circle (bhagaṇārdha).

11.03a: Due to contact with their equal mass of rays, however, the fire born from the friction of their vision, struck by the Pravaha wind, arises for the destruction of the world. 11.03b: [The fire] born from the friction of their vision, struck by the Pravaha wind, arises for the destruction of the world.
Since destruction repeatedly falls upon the worlds at this time, it is well known as *vyatīpāta*; by a different designation, it is called *vaidhṛta*.
11.05a: That Kṛṣṇa, with a terrible body, red eyes, and a large belly, 11.05b:
causing all things undesirable, the fierce one is born again and again.

11.06a–b: When the Sun and the Moon are situated at the end of the zodiacal circle and at the limit of half the circle respectively, their respective declinations are calculated by adding the degrees and so forth derived from the [observer's] latitude.

11.07a: Now, if the declination of the Moon, as it moves through odd-numbered signs, corrected by the equation of aberration, 11.07b: should be greater than the declination of the Sun, then the node has already passed.
11.08a: If [the lunar day] should be deficient, then the future [result] belongs to the left; and for the even foot, 11.08b:
there is a change of feet if it is purified by the declination and displacement of the moon.
The sines of the two latitudes, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum latitude, yield a result;
half of the arc-difference of that [result] should be added to the moon when it is about to appear.
11.10a: When the node has moved from the moon, that [longitude] multiplied by the motion of the sun, 11.10b:
divided by the lunar motion, yields a result in minutes and so forth for the sun, which is applied like that of the moon.
In the same way, the result of the moon's setting should be applied in reverse;
this process is repeated until the two [mean] longitudes are equal.

11.12a: When the two longitudes are equal, there is an eclipse; furthermore, when the Moon is diminished by the subtracted degrees, [the eclipse] has passed if it is less than midnight, and will occur if it is greater.
11.12b: [The eclipse] has passed if [the time] is less than midnight, and will occur if it is greater at that moment.

11.13a: The minutes of arc for the interval between the two, the fixed half-moon and the moon; 11.13b: multiplied by sixty and divided by the moon's velocity, yield the nāḍīs of the time of the eclipse.
11.14a: Multiply half the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon by sixty, and divide [the result] by 11.14b:
the difference between their velocities; the quotient is the duration of the eclipse in nāḍīs and so forth.
11.15a: The true mean time of immersion (pātaka) is that [mean time] diminished by the half-duration of the eclipse;
it shall be the time of its commencement. 11.15b: That [time] added to it is designated as the final [time].
11.16a: The intermediate period between the beginning and the end should be known as extremely terrible;
11.16b: blazing with the form of fire, it is censured for all ritual actions.
As long as one has entered the single path between the disks of the sun and the moon,
for that long does his birth effect the destruction of all karma.
11.18a: Through acts such as bathing, giving gifts, recitation, ancestral rites, vows, and fire offerings, 11.18b:
a very great spiritual merit is attained; likewise, [it is attained] through knowledge of the proper time.
11.19a: When the declinations of the Sun and the Moon are equal in proximity to the equinox, 11.19b:
then the node (pāta) occurs twice; in the opposite case, there is an absence [of such occurrence].
The degrees resulting from the conjunction of the moon and the sun, divided by the duration of a lunar mansion (bhoga), yield the quotient;
this is the seventeenth yoga, while the other is the third, Vyatīpāta.
