The final quarters of the asterisms of Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Revatī, as well as their junctions with the following ones, are known as *gaṇḍānta*;
the first quarter of the asterisms immediately following them is likewise proclaimed as *gaṇḍānta*.
11.22a: One should avoid the three terrible *vyatīpāta* yogas as well as the three *gaṇḍānta* junctions;
11.22b: one should likewise avoid these three *bhasandhi* junctions in all ritual activities.
11.23a: Thus has this supreme, meritorious, and beneficial account of the movements of the luminaries been told; it is a great secret. What else do you wish to hear?
12.01a: Then, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence to the one born from a portion of the Sun, 12.01b:
and having worshipped him with supreme devotion, the asura Maya asked this.
12.02a: O Blessed One, what is the extent of the earth? What is its form? What is its support? 12.02b: How is it divided, and how many are the levels of the seven netherworlds (pātāla) therein?
12.03a: And how does the sun establish the arrangement of day and night? 12.03b: How does it traverse the earth, illuminating the worlds?
12.04a: Day and night for the gods and asuras are reversed from one another. 12.04b: What is that [day], and how does it come about through the completion of the sun’s revolution through the zodiac?
12.05a: A paternal month consists of sixty *nāḍīs*, whereas a human month is likewise [defined by] sixty *nāḍīs*. 12.05b: For what reason, then, would that very same duration not apply everywhere?
12.06a: Why are the lords of the days, years, months, and hours not the same?
12.06b: How does this zodiacal circle, together with the planets, revolve, and what is its support?

12.07a: Above the earth, how high are the orbits of the planets and constellations situated one above the other, and what is the distance between them? 12.07b: What are their dimensions, and by what order are they established?
12.08a: In summer the sun possesses intense rays, but not so in winter; 12.08b: how much is the attainment of those rays, how many are the measures, and what is achieved by them?
12.09a: Thus, O Blessed One, creator of beings, cut through this doubt of mine;
12.09b: there exists no other all-seeing one who can sever it except you.
12.10a: Having heard these words spoken by him out of devotion, I then spoke this supreme secret chapter to him once again.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to this secret concerning the supreme self;
I shall proclaim it to those who possess supreme devotion, for there is nothing that I would not give to them.
Vāsudeva is the supreme Brahman; he is that form, the supreme Puruṣa, unmanifest, devoid of qualities, tranquil, beyond the twenty-fifth principle, and imperishable.
12.13a: The Lord, who is all-pervading, exists both within and without, being inherent in primordial nature (prakṛti).
12.13b: Having first created the waters, Saṅkarṣaṇa infused his seed into them.
Then there was a golden egg, enveloped everywhere in darkness;
therein the eternal Aniruddha first became manifest.
12.15a: This venerable Hiraṇyagarbha is recited in the Veda;
12.15b: for because he is the primordial source, the Sun is called Sūrya on account of his procreative power.
12.16a: "He is the supreme light beyond darkness; he is this Sun, the Savitṛ.
12.16b: As the creator of beings, he moves around the worlds, bringing them into existence.
12.17a: He is renowned as the Great One (Mahat), whose nature is luminosity and who destroys darkness;
12.17b: His sphere is the Ṛgveda, his form is the Sāmans and the Ustrās, and he is the Yajus formulas.
12.18a: This Blessed One is the great threefold Veda, the self of time, the maker of time, and the all-pervading Lord;
12.18b: He is the soul of all, omnipresent, subtle, and everything is established within him.
Having fashioned a wheel consisting of the year upon a chariot composed of all things,
he perpetually revolves with the seven meters yoked as his horses.
12.20a: Three-quarters of that nectar remained hidden; this one quarter became manifest.
12.20b: For the sake of creating the world, the Lord created Brahmā from that [quarter], who is characterized by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
Having bestowed the Vedas as boons upon him, the Grandfather of all the worlds established him within the cosmic egg and then himself moved about, contemplating him.
12.22a: Then Brahmā, bearing the form of the ego (ahaṅkāra), set his mind upon creation.
12.22b: From his mind the moon was born, and from his eyes the sun, the treasury of splendors.
From the mind [arose] space, then air, fire, water, and earth in succession;
thus the five great elements were born, each possessing an increment of one quality.
From fire and moon were born the sun and the moon; from those, Aṅgāraka and the others.
From fire, earth, ether, water, and wind, the five [planets] were born in succession.
12.25: Furthermore, the self-controlled one divided himself again twelvefold, known as the zodiac signs;
then once more, he manifested in the form of the lunar mansions, consisting of twenty-seven parts.

12.26a: Then he created the entire universe, including both the moving and the unmoving, with the gods at its head; 12.26b: subsequently, from the upper, middle, and lower streams, he brought forth the primal natures (prakṛtis).
12.27 Having created [the world] in due order as before through the differentiation of qualities and actions,
he established the divisions according to their respective natures, in accordance with the vision of the Vedas.
12.28a: The all-pervading Lord [is the cause] of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, of the earth, or of the universe;
12.28b: and likewise, in due order, of the gods, asuras, humans, and the Siddhas.
12.29a: This cosmic egg is hollow; within it are these worlds, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ.
12.29b: It has the shape of a sphere, like a casket formed by two hemispherical shells.
12.30a: Within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the surrounding boundary is called the celestial orbit (vyomakakṣā).
12.30b: In its center is the revolution of the luminaries, arranged in successive layers from below upwards.
12.31a: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon;
12.31b: these revolve one below the other, like the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and clouds.
In the center of the cosmic egg, the terrestrial globe stands in space,
sustaining the supreme power of Brahmā which consists of the capacity for support.
Within those [seven layers] are seven subterranean regions (pātāla-bhūmi), inhabited by nāgas and asuras; they are delightful and filled with the juices of divine medicinal herbs.
Mount Meru, composed of Jāmbūnada gold and a storehouse of many jewels,
situated in the center of the earth's sphere, extends out on both sides.
Above him stood the gods, including Indra, along with the great seers;
below were the Asuras, likewise, who were hostile to one another yet dependent on one another.
12.36a: Then this great ocean stands as a surrounding rim on all sides; 12.36b: like a girdle of the Earth, it effects the division between the gods and the asuras.
12.37a: Equidistant from the center of Meru on all sides, within the oceans;
12.37b: in the islands of the cardinal directions beginning with the east, there are cities fashioned by the gods.
12.38a: In the eastern quarter of the Bhūvṛtta region, there is a city renowned as Yamakoṭi; 12.38b: situated in the land of Bhadrāśva, it possesses golden ramparts and arched gateways.
12.39a: In the southern Bhārata-varṣa, there is likewise the great city of Laṅkā; 12.39b: in the western region called Ketumāla, the city known as Romaka is proclaimed.
12.40a: In the region of Kuruvarṣa, there is a city renowned by the name Udakasiddhapurī.
12.40b: In that city dwell the high-souled Siddhas, who are free from all suffering.
The cavities between the circular foot-continents are supported by one another;
and rising above them stands Mount Meru, which is equal in extent and serves as the abode of the gods.
12.42a: Above them passes the sun situated at the equinox;
12.42b: in those [regions], neither equinoctial shadow nor elevation of the pole star is observed.
12.43a: On both sides of Meru, in the middle of the sky, the pole star is situated;
12.43b: for those residing in the equatorial region, it rests upon both horizons.
12.44a: Therefore, there is no rising of the asterisms for those two poles situated on the terrestrial horizon.
12.44b: At Meru, however, the latitude is ninety degrees, and likewise the colatitude is zero degrees.
12.45a: When the Sun is in Aries or other signs located in the northern hemisphere, it becomes visible to the gods.
But for the Asuras, at the beginning of Libra and so forth, the Sun moves through those respective degrees.
12.46a: Because of its extreme proximity, it [the sun] possesses intense rays during the summer;
12.46b: but in the winter, for the gods in the region of the gods (devabhāga), it is otherwise, being of mild intensity.
12.47a: At the equinox, the gods and the asuras see the sun situated on the horizon. 12.47b: To these [beings], day and night are respectively on the left and the right.
12.48a: When the sun has risen in Aries and the other signs, moving northward through three zodiacal signs, it fulfills the forenoon for the inhabitants of Meru until midday.
12.48b: Moving [further], it fills the forenoon for those dwelling on Mount Meru until the middle of the day.
12.49a: Moving through Cancer and the subsequent signs, he likewise traverses the latter half of the day.
12.49b: Likewise, he moves through Libra and the next three signs, as well as Capricorn and the following three, for the enemies of the gods (the demons).
12.50a: Therefore, day and night for them are indeed reversed from one another;
12.50b: and the measure of a day and night [for the gods] is due to the completion of the sun's revolution through the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa).
At the end of their solstices, due to the reversal [of the seasons],
these gods and asuras cause themselves and one another to be above and below for half a day and night.
12.52a: Others, who abide by the *Sama-sūtra*, also consider [the worlds] to be situated one below the other;
12.52b: those residing in Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla, and those dwelling in Laṅkā and Siddhapura.
12.53a: On the entire terrestrial globe, one's own location is situated at the zenith;
12.53b: since the sphere is in the sky, where is its top and where is its bottom?

12.54a: Due to their small stature, people see this earth from every direction as it extends from their own location; 12.54b: even though it is circular, they perceive it as being shaped like a wheel.
12.55a: To the gods it revolves counter-clockwise; to the enemies of the gods, clockwise.
12.55b: This sphere of the stars (bhagola) is always above, facing westward at the equator.

12.56a: Therefore, in that place, the day consists of thirty nāḍīs, and likewise the year; 12.56b: the decrease and increase always occur in the left [side] for the divisions of the gods and the asuras.

12.57a: In Aries and the following signs, there is always an increase in the north, and it is greater in the northern direction. 12.57b: During the portion of the gods (the waxing fortnight), there is a decrease in the night; the opposite is true during the portion of the asuras (the waning fortnight).

12.58a: At the beginning of Libra and other signs, the decrease and increase of day and night occur respectively on the left [side]; both of these are always known through the influence of the sun's transit across regions, as previously explained. 12.58b: Their precise understanding is based on that which was stated before.
The circumference of the earth multiplied by the degrees of the sun's declination and divided by the degrees in a zodiacal circle (360),
when multiplied by the resulting yojanas, indicates how far the sun travels above the equator.
12.60a: One should thus subtract the maximum distances;
12.60b: by means of those remaining *yojanas* from a quarter of the earth's circumference.
12.61a: At the end of the solstices, for the divisions of the gods and the asuras, [the day and night] proceed in reverse order;
12.61b: by sixty nāḍīs there is one day and night, and likewise once in this [period].
Even within that interval, at the end of the sixty [nāḍīs], there is the decrease and increase of day and night;
beyond that, this sphere of the stars (bhagola) revolves in the opposite manner.
12.63a: But when the terrestrial circumference is deficient by the yojanas of twice the sine of the amplitude, 12.63b:
the sun, situated in Capricorn in the eastern quarter, is not visible.
Likewise, when situated in Gemini or Cancer during the portion of the Asuras,
one should predict the appearance [of Rāhu] at the foot of the terrestrial sphere where its shadow has vanished.
When the fourth part of the terrestrial circumference is diminished by the *yojanas* derived from the single sine and declination,
the remainder in *yojanas* is [the distance] from the equator.

12.66a: When the sun is situated in the signs of Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, it is not visible. 12.66b: But for the Asuras, it is not visible when the sun is in the four signs beginning with Taurus in the quarter of the gods.

12.67a: On Mount Meru, during the half-orbit beginning with Aries, the gods behold the sun; (during the other half-orbit) 12.67b: likewise, the asuras behold it when it has risen only once, situated in Libra and the subsequent signs.
12.68a: Then, in the fifteenth part above the terrestrial sphere, whether among the gods or the asuras;
12.68b: the sun moves above, reaching the end of the northern and southern solstices.
12.69a: The shadow between those two [halves] occurs toward the south or the north;
12.69b: it moves toward Mount Meru, and beyond that, within its own respective divisions.
12.70a: When the sun is above Bhadrāśva, it rises over Bhārata;
12.70b: meanwhile, it is midnight in Ketumāla and sunset in Kuru.

12.71a: Wandering in the same manner through the regions beginning with Bhārata, 12.71b: one should perform the circumambulation [of the sun], producing the times of midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset.
The elevation of the stellar sphere is constant for one proceeding toward Meru;
for one traveling toward the equator, the depression and elevation are the reverse.
The stellar sphere is bound between the two poles and set in motion by the Pravaha winds;
it revolves incessantly, and the orbits of the planets are attached to it in their proper order.
12.74a: The gods and asuras see the sun for half a year after it has once risen; 12.74b: the ancestors [see it] while it dwells in the moon for a fortnight, and men on earth for their own day.
12.75a: For one standing above, the armpit is large, while for one situated below it is small;
12.75b: By means of a large armpit, the portions are large, and likewise, by means of a small one, they are small.
12.76a: A planet situated in a small orbit traverses a circle of asterisms (*bhagaṇa*) in a short time; 12.76b: [whereas] a planet revolving in a large orbit does so in a long time.
The moon, moving in a small orbit, traverses many lunar mansions (bhagaṇas);
whereas Śanaiścara (Saturn), moving in a large orbit, traverses only a few of them.
12.78a: From the slowest [planet] onwards in order, the fourth planets from each are the lords of the days;
12.78b: likewise, the third planets from each are proclaimed to be the lords of the years.

12.79a: The lords of the months of the moon are traditionally held to be [determined] in an upward sequence. 12.79b: Likewise, the lords of the horās are [determined] in order, starting from Saturn and moving downward.
The circumference of the sun’s orbit, multiplied by sixty, constitutes one bhagakṣā;
the orbital sphere rotates above all others at that distance in yojanas.
The number of lunar revolutions stated for an eon, when multiplied by the lunar orbit, is to be known as the orbit of space; likewise, it is the extent of the sun's rays.
That same [number], when divided by the number of kalpas and planetary revolutions, becomes their revolution;
when divided by the *kuvāsara*s (intercalary days), it is recorded as the eastward motion of all the days.
The number of yojanas for one day's motion, multiplied by the Moon's revolution [in days],
and divided by its own orbit, yields its daily motion in liptās when further divided by the number of lunar days (tithis).

12.84a: The girth (kakṣā), multiplied by the radius of the earth and divided by the circumference of the terrestrial sphere, [yields the distance from the center]. 12.84b: That radius, diminished by the terrestrial radius, halved, gives the respective height of the planet's apogee.
12.85a: The revolutions of the moon are fifteen thousand, four hundred and thirty-two (32,430).
12.85b: Those of the swift-moving Mercury are one million, four hundred and thirty-two thousand, nine hundred and forty-three (1,043,209).
12.86a: And those of the swift-moving Venus are twenty-six million, six hundred and forty-six thousand, three hundred and seventy (26,646,370).
12.86b: Then, for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, [the values are] zero, zero, eight, one, and four oceans (4331500).
12.87a: For Mars as well, they are nine, zero, nine, six, four, one, and serpents (8146909).
12.87b: For the Moon's apogee, they are four, eight, four, oceans, earth, two, three, and eight fires (38328484).
12.88a: For Jupiter, [the revolutions] are five thousand seven hundred sixty-four thousand five hundred seventy-six (5,137,576).
12.88b: For Rāhu, they are eight hundred fifty-seven thousand two hundred eighty-six (857,286).
12.89a: Then for Saturn, they are one hundred twenty-seven million six hundred sixty-eight thousand two hundred fifty-five (127,668,255).
12.89b: [The number of] light-years is 12,890,012;
(259,800,12). 12.90b: This is the circumference of the rotation of the cosmic egg’s shell, while the extent of the sun’s rays reaches everywhere within it.
[The Jyotiṣopaniṣad] 13.01a: Now, having bathed and being pure and adorned, in a secret and clean place;
13.01b: having worshipped with devotion the Sun, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the Guhyakas.
13.02a: Through the traditional instruction as it was received from the mouth of the Guru according to his knowledge;
13.02b: the Teacher, having perceived everything directly, [taught] all this for the sake of awakening the disciple.
13.03a: One should construct a marvelous model of the terrestrial globe;
13.03b: having first fashioned a desired terrestrial sphere out of wood.
The staff (axis) passes through the center of Meru, extending out on both sides;
likewise, there are two supporting orbits and the equatorial orbit.

13.05a: Those three [lines] should be made in finger-breadths according to the degrees of the asterism (bhagaṇa), halved; 13.05b: and by means of the hypotenuses (karṇa) of their respective half-daily periods, according to the inference of those proportions.
And by the degrees of obliquity and declination, halved and directed southward or northward,
one should [calculate] the three [sines] for Aries and the other signs from their respective obliquities.
13.07a: One should determine those girths (kakṣās) for Cancer and the others in reverse order;
13.07b: likewise, three for Libra and the others, and for Capricorn and the others in the opposite manner.

13.08a: For both [the sun and the moon], the [ecliptic] orbits situated on the southern hemisphere should be constructed starting from the support of the apogee (kakṣādhāra). 13.08b: Likewise for the stars situated on the southern and northern hemispheres, as well as for Abhijit.
13.09a: One should arrange [the orbits] of the Seven Sages, Agastya, Brahmā, and the others; 13.09b:
the equinoctial orbit indeed stands in the middle of all of them.
13.10a: Then, after the conjunction with the support, there are two equinoxes in the [northern and southern] courses;
13.10b: from the position of the equinox, by means of the precise degrees resulting from the movement through the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa).
13.11a: One should thus determine the fields for goats and other animals by means of diagonal cords (tiryag-jyā).
13.11b: From one course (ayana) to another course, there is likewise another lateral enclosure (kakṣā).
13.12a: By that [revolution] known as *krānti*, the Sun always revolves, illuminating [the world]; 13.12b:
and the Moon and the other [planets] likewise revolve by means of their own nodes (*pāta*) situated upon the eccentric circle (*apamaṇḍala*).

13.13a: Then, due to their deviation from the path, they are seen drawn away at the ends of their dispersion; 13.13b: by virtue of that, the ascendant rises at the eastern horizon and sets accordingly.
13.14a: According to the established method using the longitudinal differences (laṅkodayas), that which is situated at the center above the middle of the sky [is the meridian];
13.14b: the sine (jyā) between the middle of the celestial equator and the horizon is designated as the "final" (antyā).
13.15a: The sine of the car-quarter (caradalajyā) should be known as the interval between the equator and the horizon;
13.15b: having placed one's own position above, with the circle of the horizon in the middle.
Covered externally by a cloth and encircled by the Lokāloka mountain,
it is the means for the rotation of time through the application of the flow of nectar.
13.17a: One should construct a Golayantra (celestial sphere instrument) joined with a tall seed-pipe.
13.17b: Though this has been explained openly, it must be kept secret; otherwise, it would become accessible to everyone here.
13.18a: Therefore, one should construct the supreme *gola* according to the instruction of a teacher;
13.18b: for in every age, this construction of Vivasvat has been interrupted.
13.19a: Through the grace of someone else, it may further manifest according to one's desire;
13.19b: likewise, one should accomplish mechanical devices for the purpose of regulating time.
13.20a: Alone, one should apply the seed-syllable to the wondrous machine;
13.20b: by means of pegs, rods, bows, wheels, and various shadow-machines.
13.21a: The knowledge of time should be understood from the instructions of the guru by those who are unwearied;
13.21b: by means of water-machines, skull-cups, and so forth, as well as peacocks, men, and monkeys.
And one should properly adorn it at the right time with threads and powders placed within.
Mercury, women, water, and thread; copper, oil, and water; seeds, and dust—in these, those applications are also difficult to obtain.
A copper vessel with a hole at the bottom, placed in a basin of pure water, sinks sixty times in a day and night; this is clearly the *kapālaka* instrument.
13.24a: Likewise, the Narayantra is excellent for use during the day when the sun is clear;
13.24b: it is declared to be the supreme means for determining time through the calculation of shadows.
Having understood the movements of the planets and constellations and the sphere (gola) according to its true nature,
the self-possessed man attains the world of the planets in due course.
The Brahma, the Divine, the Pitrya, the Prajapatya,
the Gauri, the Saura, the Savana, the Chandra, and the Arksha— these indeed are the nine measures of time.
14.02a: Here, the calculation is conducted by means of four [calendars]: the solar, the lunar, the sidereal, and the civil;
14.02b: the sixty-year cycle is to be understood through the Bārhaspatya [cycle], but never by others.

14.03a: By solar [calculation], one determines the measure of day and night, as well as the six *aśītimukha* periods; 14.03b: the two solstices (*ayana*) and the equinox (*viṣuvat*), and the auspiciousness of the time at the moment of transit (*saṃkrānti*).
14.04a: The six *ṣaḍaśīti* days beginning with Libra are, in order, the openings of the *ṣaḍaśīti* periods;
14.04b: these four alone occur within the zodiac signs of dual nature.
In the twenty-sixth part of Dhanus, in the twenty-second of Nimiṣa,
in the eighteenth part of Mithuna, and in the fourteenth of Kanyā.
14.06a: Furthermore, those sixteen days of the daughter that remain thereafter, 14.06b: are equal to sacrificial rites; what is given to the ancestors on them becomes inexhaustible.
At the hub of the wheel of the zodiac, the two equinoxes lie on a common meridian line, as do the two solstices; these four are indeed well-known.
In the intervals between those, there are two pairs of transits;
due to the continuity of the transit, these should be known as the two Viṣṇupadīs.

14.09a: From the sun's entry into Capricorn, there are six months of the northern course (uttarāyaṇa). 14.09b: But from Cancer and so forth, likewise, there are six months of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
The lords of the two signs are the seasons (*ṛtu*); from them come the [six] starting with *śiśira*.
These twelve, beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), are the months; by means of these alone is the year constituted.
The minutes of the solar measure, multiplied by sixty and divided by the [daily] motion, yield half-nāḍīs; the period prior to the saṅkrānti as well as that following it is meritorious.
14.12a: When the moon, having emerged from the sun, moves toward the east day after day;
14.12b: that is the lunar measure (cāndramāna); it should be known that a lunar day (tithi) consists of twelve parts (aṃśas).
14.13a: The lunar day (tithi), the karana, marriage, shaving, and likewise all ritual acts;
14.13b: as well as the performance of vows, fasts, and journeys, are governed by the lunar month.
14.14a: Thirty lunar days (tithis) constitute a month, which is recorded as a day of the ancestors (pitryam ahaḥ).
14.14b: And the night [of that day] is at the end of the month and the fortnight; the division between these two occurs in their midst.
14.15a: The constant revolution of the stellar sphere is called a lunar day (nākṣatra-dina).
14.15b: The months, however, are to be known by the names of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), according to their conjunction at the end of the [lunar] phases.
14.16a: In the conjunctions beginning with Kārttika, two pairs starting with Kṛttikā [are assigned];
14.16b: the last, the penultimate, and the fifth [nakṣatras] are traditionally held to constitute the three months in three ways.
14.17a: In the dark fortnights of Vaiśākha and the other months, there is a conjunction on the fifteenth lunar day.
14.17b: Likewise, the years beginning with Kārttika are determined from the heliacal setting or rising of Jupiter.

14.18a: That which is from sunrise to sunrise is proclaimed as the solar (sāvana) day. 14.18b: By means of these solar days, the rules for the timing of sacrifices are established. 14.19a: Likewise, the determination of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and so forth, as well as days, months, years, and seasons [are measured by them].
14.19b: However, the mean motion of the planets is determined by the solar day alone.

14.20a: That which is declared as a day and night for the gods and demons, occurring through their reversal [of time], 14.20b: that constitutes a divine (divya) year, resulting from the completion of the sun’s revolution through the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa).
The regulation of the Manvantaras is declared to be that of Prajāpati;
therein there is no distinction between day and night, for it is proclaimed as the Brāhma Kalpa.
14.22a: This supreme secret, most wonderful, has been declared to you;
14.22b: this is the supreme Brahman, meritorious, and the destroyer of all sins.
14.23a: Having demonstrated the supreme knowledge of the celestial bodies, the bears, and the planets;
14.23b: having understood [this], one attains an eternal station in the worlds of the sun and other luminaries.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of Maya, who honored him in return,
he, whose splendor was like that of the sun, ascended to heaven and entered his own celestial sphere.
14.25a: Then, having directly realized that divine knowledge from Vivasvat, 14.25b:
he considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose, with all taints shaken off.
Then, having learned that Maya had obtained a boon from the Sun, the seers approached him and,
surrounding him, questioned him about his knowledge with great respect.
14.27a: Delighted, he imparted to them the great course of the planets;
14.27b: most wonderful in the world, a secret equal to the Veda.
